notes.trap: An empty string returns 0, not NULL, so you cannot use `ascii(...)` to tell an empty string apart from a string that starts with the NUL character.
The count is based on the UTF-8 encoded bytes, not on characters. Any non-ASCII character adds 16 or more bits instead of 8.
The second argument is a set of characters, not a substring. Any mix of those characters is stripped from both ends.
Only the low 8 bits of the argument are used (n & 255), so values above 255 silently wrap around instead of producing a Unicode code point or an error.
A negative argument returns an empty string, not NULL and not an error.
For BINARY input it counts bytes, not characters. Wrapping a string in `encode(...)` therefore changes the result for non-ASCII text, and the result then matches `octet_length(...)`.
Numeric arguments are implicitly cast to STRING before measuring. A double such as 1E3 becomes '1000.0', so you get the length of its string form, not the number of digits.
NULL arguments and NULL array elements are skipped, unlike `concat(...)` which returns NULL. Empty strings are not skipped, so they still produce consecutive separators.
The match is case-sensitive, and an empty search string always returns true.
In the search/result form, NULL matches a NULL search value, unlike CASE x WHEN NULL. With exactly two arguments it is a different function entirely: it decodes bytes using a charset.
With ANSI mode off (the default), an index of 0, a negative index or an index past the end returns NULL silently instead of raising an error. Indexes are 1-based.
The 'utf-16' charset produces a big-endian byte order mark (FEFF) before the data. Use 'UTF-16BE' or 'UTF-16LE' if you need the bytes without a BOM.
List items are not trimmed, so a space after a comma becomes part of the item. A missing match returns 0, not NULL.
It returns a STRING with thousands separators, not a rounded number, so the result cannot be used directly in arithmetic or numeric sorting. Use `round(...)` when you need a numeric value.
NULL arguments do not make the result NULL. They are formatted as the literal text 'null'.
Only spaces start a new word. Letters after hyphens, underscores or apostrophes stay lowercase, and all other letters are forced to lowercase.
The match is case-sensitive and returns 0, not NULL, when the substring is not found. The argument order is (str, substr), which is the reverse of `locate(...)`.
